newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Europe's transit system under threat - EU's Monti.
newsitem.headline: Europe's transit system under threat - EU's Monti.

text.p: Organised crime is threatening the system designed by the European Union to ease red tape on taxable goods that are shipped across borders, EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti said on Thursday.

"The greatest threat to transit is organised crime, which seems to be better organised on an international basis than either customs or the legitimate trade," Monti told a conference on how to reform Europe's fraud-ridden transit system.
The EU system allows traders to pay customs duties, value-added tax and excise duties in the country of final destination, rather than at borders in between.
But fraudulent operators offload goods such as alcohol and tobacco on the market before arriving in the city where the taxes must be paid.

"Fraudsters, hidden behind the increasing flow of trade between all parts of Europe, have quickly seen all the benefits they could draw," Monti said. "This is because the facilities offered do not yet have a sufficient counterpart in terms of prevention and control.
The two-day "Eurotransit '97" conference, which started on Thursday, gathered representatives from the European Union executive, member states, other European countries and industry.

There is wide agreement that the transit system -- designed in the 1960s -- has not kept up with changes such as the removal of EU internal border checks in 1993 and expansion of the system to non-EU European countries.
According to EU figures, fraud amounted to at least 750 million European currency units ($880 million) in the period 1990-1994.

"It seems to revolve essentially around contraband, theft of goods, and falsification of documents or official stamps," said secretary general Zygmunt Tyszkiewicz of the European employers federation UNICE.

John Tomlinson, a British Socialist who chairs a European Parliament committee of inquiry into the EU transit system, described it as too slow, too fraud-prone and "completely unsuitable for the single market."
"What we have now is a single market in which goods cross borders, criminals cross borders but public authorities still seem to stop at borders," he said.
Monti, whose staff is preparing an action plan to reform the system, called for more cooperation to combat fraud.
"How can we master this attack, unless we are able to pass on intelligence, unless we learn to cooperate effectively and learn to talk to each other?"

He said increased flexibility for trade must be combined with improved customs controls. "This should be done by using our imagination in harnessing the new technologies of communication and computerisation."
A computerisation project initiated by the Commission is supposed to be in place by the end of 1998.
Other speakers agreed with the need for modernisation.
"Our transit system is still working with pencil and paper," said D.E. Witteveen, director-general of tax policy and customs legislation in the Netherlands. "We have to move forward."
UNICE's Tyszkiewicz, saying transit was vital for corporate competitiveness, said the system was in crisis and it was up to the Commission to "repair the damage".
He said a system was needed that cut down on fraud without "penalising the large majority of honest operators."
